name: Traditional Breads
description: Iranian bread traditions encompass thin flatbreads, thicker breakfast breads, and regional varieties made with different grains and cooking surfaces. Understanding their textures and baking techniques reveals a food culture considerably broader than a single national loaf.

seo.title: Traditional Iranian Breads: Flatbreads and Regional Baking
seo.description: Explore sangak, barbari, lavash and taftoon, alongside regional Iranian breads and the techniques that distinguish them.

content.heading: Bread as part of the meal
content.content: The Persian word *nan* means bread, but it also carries a wider association with eating: historical Persian expressions using the word can mean having a meal. Bread is therefore a useful starting point for understanding everyday Iranian cooking. Its role extends beyond an accompaniment placed beside a finished dish. Sangak, for example, can be torn into the broth of *abgoosht*, a meat-and-pulse dish, before the remaining solids are mashed and eaten separately with bread. [s1]

content.heading: Recognizing the familiar varieties
content.content: Four names recur in accounts of Iranian bakeries: sangak, barbari, taftoon and lavash. Sangak takes its name from the small stones covering its baking surface; contact with those stones leaves an irregular impression. Barbari is a thicker, oval bread associated with breakfast and cheese. Lavash and taftoon belong to the thinner end of the range, although their doughs and thickness vary. Traditional oven-wall baking uses a padded support to transfer flattened dough onto the hot interior of a *tanur*, or bread oven. These differences make the baking surface as useful an identifying feature as the finished shape. [s1]

content.heading: Beyond the familiar bakery names
content.content:
Regional examples widen the picture. A review published in the Journal of Ethnic Foods describes *lako*, a rice-flour bread in Gilan on the Caspian coast, and *kalaneh* in Kurdistan, made with ingredients including scallions and cooked on a metal surface. In Hormozgan, beside the Persian Gulf, thin bread can be dressed with *mahyaweh*, a fish-based condiment. Such examples show why Iranian bread cannot be described entirely through wheat flour and a single oven design. [s2]

The same review describes Mazandaran's *kelichehnoon*, a small bread associated with ceremonial use and keeping for journeys. Its recipes may combine wheat and rice flour with fats, dairy ingredients or spices. Bread can thus serve different purposes: immediate eating, travel provisions, or a food associated with an occasion. Regional names identify a repertoire of practices rather than a uniform recipe followed by every household. [s2]

content.heading: A tradition with variations
content.content: Recipes should be read as documented examples rather than rigid specifications. The reviewed literature distinguishes breads by flour, additions, equipment and production method, including traditional and mechanized baking. That framework is more useful than assuming that a familiar name guarantees an identical loaf everywhere. It also keeps attention on the baker's work: shaping dough and managing its contact with heat help create the bread's identity. [s2]

name: Iranian Sweets
description: Iranian sweets include regional cookies and confections whose identities depend on ingredients, texture and preparation. Documented examples range from rice-flour cookies associated with Kermanshah to gaz, a nut-filled confection associated especially with Isfahan.

seo.title: Iranian Sweets: Regional Cookies and Gaz
seo.description: Discover documented Iranian cookie traditions, regional food gifts and the preparation of Isfahan's gaz.

content.heading: A geography of cookies
content.content:
Iranian cookies offer a useful introduction to the country's regional sweet-making. Encyclopaedia Iranica identifies rice-flour cookies, *nan-e berenji*, with Kermanshah while also documenting their reputation in Qazvin and Shiraz. Their name literally identifies rice bread, but here it denotes a delicate cookie. The documented dough combines rice flour, sugar, rose water, eggs and oil; shaping and surface impressions contribute to its appearance. [s1]

Other cookies depend on different ingredients and techniques. Roasted chickpea flour gives *nan-e nokhodchi* its identity, while northern *kolucheh* can enclose a walnut-and-honey filling. Almond cookies associated with Tabriz belong to another part of this repertoire. These examples demonstrate regional associations without establishing exclusive ownership or a single recipe for each name. [s1]

content.heading: Gaz and the confectioner's craft
content.content:
Gaz is a confection associated especially with Isfahan. Iranica's account describes a traditional preparation using *gaz-angobin*, a sweet substance obtained from Khansar, together with egg whites, sugar, and pistachios or almonds. The sweet substance is dissolved and strained; beating, heating and the addition of nuts transform the mixture before it is shaped and cooled. [s2]

Texture is central to its identity. The account describes a confection with both adhesive and brittle qualities, rather than a baked crumb. Pieces can be packed in loose flour to help prevent sticking and protect them from moisture. This also explains why flour surrounding a confection need not mean that it was baked as a flour-based cookie. [s2]

The source explicitly notes differences between confectioners, including closely guarded recipes passed between generations. Its description establishes a documented traditional method; it does not establish the ingredients of every contemporary product sold as gaz. [s2]

content.heading: Making, sharing and taking home
content.content: Sweet-making connects domestic kitchens with specialist shops. Iranica documents cookies prepared for Nowruz, the Iranian New Year, alongside varieties made for other occasions. It also describes regional cookies given as travel gifts. In that setting, a sweet carries an association with a place as well as a particular flavor. This is a more precise way to understand the examples here than treating them as one interchangeable national dessert. [s1]

name: Tea Culture
description: Tea culture in Iran connects brewing and serving practices with hospitality, workplaces and public meeting places. Its history also includes the development of domestic cultivation and the survival of the word coffeehouse for establishments that served tea.

seo.title: Tea Culture in Iran: Brewing, Hospitality and History
seo.description: Understand Iranian tea preparation, sugar on the side, historic coffeehouses and the development of domestic tea cultivation.

content.heading: From concentrated brew to a glass of tea
content.content:
Tea, *chay* in Persian, is both a beverage and a setting for social interaction. Iranica's historical account describes its presence in administrative offices and bazaar business, where serving tea accompanies work and conversation. These observations document established social habits rather than a rule followed by every Iranian. [s1]

A characteristic preparation uses black tea brewed with a little water in a small teapot, or *quri*, kept above a kettle or samovar. Concentrated tea is poured into a glass and diluted with hot water. The drinker can therefore adjust its strength: *por-rang* describes a darker, stronger glass, while *kam-rang* describes a lighter one. The familiar glass, *estekan*, is served on a saucer. [s1]

Sugar need not be stirred into the liquid. In the practice called *qand-pahlu*, sugar is served alongside the tea and may be held in the mouth while drinking. The same account records regional variations, including citrus additions and milk tea among communities in the southeast. These examples should be read as documented variation, not as a complete map of present-day preferences. [s1]

content.heading: Drinking tea and growing tea
content.content:
The history of tea drinking should be distinguished from the history of cultivating the crop inside Iran. Mohammad Mirza Kashef-al-Saltana, a diplomat and agricultural reformer, played a prominent role in promoting domestic cultivation around the turn of the twentieth century. His interest developed during service in India, where he studied agricultural practices and sent tea seeds and cultivation literature to Tehran. He also brought plants back to Iran. [s2]

The project had an economic purpose as well as a botanical one. Kashef-al-Saltana and government officials viewed domestic tea cultivation as a way to meet demand and reduce reliance on imports. His expectation that Iran could eventually become self-sufficient was an aspiration, not proof that self-sufficiency followed. The distinction matters: a successful effort to establish cultivation does not by itself demonstrate that domestic harvests subsequently supplied all tea consumed in the country. [s2]

content.heading: Why a tea-serving place might be called a coffeehouse
content.content:
The word *qahveh-khaneh* means coffeehouse. It remained in use after tea displaced coffee as the principal beverage in these establishments; *chay-khaneh*, or teahouse, also circulated. A historical name can therefore preserve an earlier drinking culture even when the contents of the cup have changed. [s3]

These venues were also meeting places. Accounts of Safavid coffeehouses describe poets, artists and other visitors gathering there, while later establishments hosted recitations and storytelling. Their significance lay partly in the social activity around the beverage. A teapot alone cannot explain the institution: conversation, performance and the availability of a shared meeting space were integral to its history. [s3]

Historical descriptions nevertheless require care. The encyclopedia account discusses particular periods and establishments, including spaces strongly associated with male sociability. It does not establish the clientele or atmosphere of every contemporary café. Tea culture is best understood through several connected histories: preparing a drink, welcoming company, operating public meeting places and developing a domestic crop. Each illuminates a different part of the subject. [s1][s2][s3]
